name: Nandini
definition: Nandini is a composite portrait of a woman from a Vokkaliga farming family in Devanahalli taluk, Bengaluru North district (formerly Bengaluru Rural), who operates a small daily milk collection and distribution business alongside managing her household's dairy herd. She represents the experience of women in the district's villages navigating the rapid transformation of the peri-urban belt around Kempegowda International Airport, balancing agrarian livelihoods with new opportunities and pressures from industrial and aerospace-park expansion.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Nandini begins her day at four in the morning, milking the family's eight crossbred cows and two buffaloes before loading the milk cans onto her Activa scooter. By six she has collected milk from twelve neighbouring households in her village, some of them kin, and delivers the combined morning run to the Nandini dairy chilling centre three kilometres away on the Devanahalli-Bangalore highway. She returns home to prepare breakfast, feed the calves, and clean the cattle shed before her older son leaves for school. In the afternoon she repeats a smaller evening collection round. Her husband manages their five-acre holding—hybrid ragi, a coconut grove, and fodder—and works intermittent contract labour at a nearby logistics warehouse serving the airport. The dairy business brings in roughly eight thousand rupees a month after deductions; the warehouse wage is irregular but sometimes adds another six thousand. Land values have risen sharply as aerospace firms and real-estate developers acquire plots, but selling would leave them without a livelihood, so they hold on. Diesel, cattle-feed prices, and veterinary costs have all climbed; the milk price the dairy pays has not kept pace.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Nandini lives in a joint household with her husband, their two sons (aged thirteen and nine), her mother-in-law, and her husband's unmarried younger brother. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties, used to manage the cattle but arthritis has made milking painful, so Nandini took over the route seven years ago. Her husband's brother works night shifts at the airport as a baggage handler and sleeps during the day. Nandini's own parents farm in a village near Hoskote; she visits them every few months. Her marriage was arranged when she was twenty-one, after she finished second PUC. Household decisions—what to plant, whether to sell a calf, how much to spend on her sons' tuition—are made jointly with her husband, though her mother-in-law's voice still carries weight on domestic matters. Cooking, cleaning, and helping the boys with homework fall to Nandini. Her younger son has mild asthma; she watches his breathing carefully during the winter haze. The family speaks Kannada at home; her sons switch to English phrases picked up at school and from television.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Nandini studied in the government Kannada-medium school in her natal village through tenth standard, then attended a government junior college in town for PUC, travelling by KSRTC bus. She did well enough in her second PUC exams to consider a BCom degree, but her parents could not afford hostel fees in Bangalore, and marriage came soon after. Her older son attends a private English-medium school in Devanahalli town; the fees are twelve thousand rupees a year, plus books, uniform, and transport. Her younger son is in the same school. She chose it because the village government school has frequent teacher vacancies and she worries the boys will not learn enough English to compete for jobs. The school runs a van; she pays fifteen hundred rupees per child per term. She wants both sons to finish degree college, ideally engineering, so they will not depend on farming or manual labour. Tuition classes cost another two thousand rupees a month for the older boy. The family has taken a small loan from a relative to cover this year's fees. She herself wishes she had continued to degree level; she feels the lack when helping with homework.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: The family depends on the government primary health centre in the village for vaccinations, fever, and minor injuries; the ANM visits monthly. For anything serious they go to the taluk hospital in Devanahalli town, a thirty-minute bus ride, or to a private clinic there if they can afford it. Nandini's younger son's asthma is managed with an inhaler prescribed by a private doctor; the monthly cost of the inhaler and check-ups runs to eight hundred rupees. Her mother-in-law's arthritis has worsened; government hospital doctors advised physiotherapy, but the nearest centre is in Bangalore and they cannot afford repeated trips. Nandini herself had an ovarian cyst diagnosed two years ago at a free health camp; surgery at the district hospital was free under Ayushman Bharat but follow-up was poor and she still has intermittent pain. She worries about her husband's occasional chest pain—he smokes beedis—but he refuses to see a doctor. The village borewell water has high nitrate levels according to a Jal Jeevan Mission test; they boil and filter drinking water. Truck traffic and dust from road-widening projects aggravate her son's asthma. She keeps tulsi and neem in the yard and uses home remedies for colds.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Nandini's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, which is numerically strong and socially dominant in the village. Caste ties shape whom they lend to, borrow from, and do business with; most of her milk-collection clients are Vokkaliga households. The village has a small Anjaneya temple where she lights a lamp on Saturdays, and a annual jatra in Chaitra for the gramadevata that draws everyone regardless of caste. Her mother-in-law observes all major festivals—Ugadi, Varamahalakshmi, Deepavali—and Nandini manages the cooking and preparations. The family has loose ties to the Adichunchanagiri Mutt in Nagamangala; they attended a mass-marriage event there once, years ago. Village social life revolves around family functions, the temple, and self-help-group meetings. Nandini joined a women's SHG four years ago; it meets monthly in the anganwadi and handles small savings and loans. She borrowed twenty thousand rupees from the group to repair the cattle shed. The SHG also organises health camps and government-scheme information sessions. Village elders, mostly older Vokkaliga men, still settle land and water disputes informally.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Nandini's household receives subsidised rice and ragi under Anna Bhagya from the fair-price shop in the village; her Ayushman Bharat card covered her surgery. She has used the Shakti free-bus scheme occasionally to visit the district hospital or her parents, saving fifty or sixty rupees each trip, though the milk route still requires her scooter. Her husband gets some MGNREGA work during the monsoon when warehouse shifts dry up, but the job cards often show phantom muster rolls and payments are delayed. The gram panchayat has not held elections in years; the same unofficial headman, a retired teacher, liaises with the taluk office. She has never met the tahsildar or MLA. A Jal Jeevan Mission tap-connection promise from two years ago has not materialised; the panchayat says funds were diverted. The dairy payments come through her bank account; she opened it under a financial-inclusion drive and now uses it for SHG transactions. Land records are online under Bhoomi, but when a neighbour's boundary was disputed the tahsildar's office demanded a bribe she could not afford. She does not follow state politics closely but knows Siddaramaiah is chief minister and that the government has promised the five guarantees.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Nandini is proud of her village's farming heritage and her family's ability to keep the dairy herd going despite rising costs and shrinking margins. She worries constantly about money—school fees, cattle feed, medical bills—and whether the land will stay in the family or be sold to a developer if her sons pursue city jobs and lose interest in farming. The airport and the aerospace park have brought jobs, but most go to outsiders with English and technical skills; local youth get only contract labour or security posts. She resents that milk prices have stagnated while everything else has become more expensive, and that the Nandini dairy's payments are sometimes delayed without explanation. She blames middlemen and government neglect of farmers, though she is grateful for Ayushman Bharat. Her greatest hope is that her sons will study well, get stable salaried jobs, and not have to depend on the weather or the mercy of a chilling centre. She fears her younger son's asthma will worsen with the air quality, and that her husband's occasional drinking and smoking will lead to serious illness they cannot afford to treat. She wishes she had more say in village decisions and that the gram panchayat were more accountable.
